biology, timing of the annual cycle, fledgling success, foods and foraging ecology; all aspects
of a species’ b iology th at are imp ortant wh en it comes to con ser vat ion man agement, vary
region to region and even year to year. Further research at multiple sites is required into all
these aspects of their ecology.

During the breeding season l  ittle penguins generally feed within about 20 km of their colony
although tracking studies show that at some sites penguins may fed much further offshore.
It is assumed they travel further between breeding  seasons, although there  is  no New
Zealand data to  confirm this. The penguins from Australian research sites forage in very
different marine environments from those utilised by New Zealand penguins, and ashore are
exposed to different predators and climates. Furthermore, the Australian birds perhaps
belong to a different  taxon than those  inhabiting most of New  Zealand.

Little penguins are subject to numerous threats both on land and at sea. Ashore the main
threats include dogs  (Canis familiaris), road-kill, introduced predators, coastal development
and disturbance from people. Marine threats include  entanglement  in fishing  nets,  changes
in food availability due to fishing, climate change and ocean warming. Threats vary from
region to region, although most information available is anecdotal and there have been few
att e mpts to quantify threats.

Conservation needs may differ region to region necessitating regional or population level
management.  Only a comprehensive, investigative approach will allow u s to u nd erstand
factors driving declines and identify and enact the management actions required to reverse
declines of  Little penguins  in different parts  of New Zealand.

In this report we review the current knowledge of this species in New Zealand, identify gaps
in our knowledge and research priorities required to allow evidence-based  conservation of
the species. We use the name l  ittle penguin  to  refe r t o a ll members of the genus Eudyptula
and present here information on all New Zealand Eudyptula  populations. As the location of
each study cited is given, it should be simple to assign information to a species/sub  -species
once the  taxonomy  is finally  re s o l ved  and the geographical limits of the proposed
Australian/Otago taxa  determined.

Previous reviews o f  Little penguin bi o logy an d pr iority li sts

There are numerous books on penguins catering for both the scientific and popular markets
and most  have  sections devoted to l  ittle penguins (among the best are Davis & Renner 2003
an d  t he  th ree  chapters on  little penguins in De Roy et  al  . 2013); most use information from
Australian studies  with the  implicit assumption that things  will be  similar in  New  Zealand.
The account in Marchant & Higgins (1990) is the most encyclopaedic including snippets of
information from all parts of their range.  A concise summary of the status of the specie s a nd
the basis for this appears in Birdlife (2017). The best recent review of current  knowled ge is b y
Peter Dann (2013), based mostly on his many years working with l  ittle penguins at Phillip
Island in Australia. His account is Australian focused and, while an excellent over view, lacks

Con ser vation statu s

The Department of Conservation lists the l  ittle penguin as ‘at risk -  declining’ (Robertson et
al., 2017) and the IUCN Red List as ‘le a st co n ce rn  ’ (BirdLife  2017). Both organisations
recognise a single species with no sub-species. The status of th e New Zealan d  taxon is likely
to change if two species/s u  b  -species we re re co gn ise d .

Ta  x  o  n  o  m  y

An article published in a New Zealand magazine in 2014 discussed one of these birds, which exhibited bizarre behavior by attacking a black pennant on a yacht on the morning of the 18th of February 2014. ## Introduction

Gray Petrels have a circumpolar distribution in the Southern Ocean, with breeding colonies found from Tristan da Cunha and Gough Island east through the Indian Ocean to Campbell and Antipodes Island. These bulky bodied petrels are distinctively patterned with their whitish underbody contrasting with the drab gray underwing and upperparts. Nests of the Gray Petrel are found in burrows on islands with steep vegetated slopes. After breeding, Gray Petrels disperse across the Southern Ocean reaching the subtropical zone by following the cold Humboldt and Bengeula Currents. These petrels mostly feed on squid and fish, which they catch by surface seizing and pursuit-plunging.Gray Petrels sometimes feed in large flocks that associate with large marine mammals, and will also follow ships. Although not globally threatened, these birds are susceptible to introduced predators and human disturbance.

## Introduction

Gray Petrels have a circumpolar distribution in the Southern Ocean, with breeding colonies found from Tristan da Cunha and Gough Island east through the Indian Ocean to Campbell and Antipodes Island. These bulky bodied petrels are distinctively patterned with their whitish underbody contrasting with the drab gray underwing and upperparts. Nests of the Gray Petrel are found in burrows on islands with steep vegetated slopes. After breeding, Gray Petrels disperse across the Southern Ocean reaching the subtropical zone by following the cold Humboldt and Bengeula Currents. These petrels mostly feed on squid and fish, which they catch by surface seizing and pursuit-plunging.Gray Petrels sometimes feed in large flocks that associate with large marine mammals, and will also follow ships. Although not globally threatened, these birds are susceptible to introduced predators and human disturbance.

There is a marine bird that gets its name from the markings that appear on its feathers during the breeding season. An article published in a New Zealand magazine in 2014 discussed one of these birds, which exhibited bizarre behavior by attacking a black pennant on a yacht on the morning of the 18th of February 2014. ## Northern Gannet Photos and Videos

Previous

[![Image 21: Shape of the Northern Gannet](https://www.allaboutbirds.org/guide/assets/photo/66025421-720px.jpg) ### Adult](https://www.allaboutbirds.org/guide/Northern_Gannet/photo-gallery/66025421)

Large heavy-bodied seabird with a daggerlike bill. Adults are mostly white with a yellowish wash on the head and neck and black flight feathers.

[© John Reynolds / Macaulay Library](https://macaulaylibrary.org/photo/41713381)Occitanie, December 03, 2016

[![Image 22: Northern Gannet](https://www.allaboutbirds.org/guide/assets/photo/66025411-720px.jpg) ### Juvenile](https://www.allaboutbirds.org/guide/Northern_Gannet/photo-gallery/66025411)

Large seabird. Juveniles are brown overall with white spotting.

[© John Reynolds / Macaulay Library](https://macaulaylibrary.org/photo/41713461)Occitanie, December 03, 2016

[![Image 23: Northern Gannet](https://www.allaboutbirds.org/guide/assets/videoThumbs/360242481-720px.jpg) ### Courtship](https://www.allaboutbirds.org/guide/Northern_Gannet/photo-gallery/360242481)

Pairs are monogamous and mate for life. They maintain pair bonds by performing a variety of displays each time they reunite at the nest site.

[© Frédérick Lelièvre / Macaulay Library](https://macaulaylibrary.org/video/360242481)Quebec, July 21, 2021

[![Image 24: Color pattern of the Northern Gannet](https://www.allaboutbirds.org/guide/assets/photo/66025391-720px.jpg) ### Adult](https://www.allaboutbirds.org/guide/Northern_Gannet/photo-gallery/66025391)

Bullet-shaped seabird with long pointed wings and long tail. In flight note white body and black flight feathers.

[© Dorian Anderson / Macaulay Library](https://macaulaylibrary.org/photo/28586791)Newfoundland and Labrador, July 02, 2013

[![Image 25: Northern Gannet](https://www.allaboutbirds.org/guide/assets/photo/66025401-720px.jpg) ### Juvenile](https://www.allaboutbirds.org/guide/Northern_Gannet/photo-gallery/66025401)

Juveniles in flight are brown overall with a white patch on the tail.

[© John Reynolds / Macaulay Library](https://macaulaylibrary.org/photo/41713571)Occitanie, December 03, 2016

[![Image 26: Northern Gannet](https://www.allaboutbirds.org/guide/assets/videoThumbs/646780637-720px.jpg) ### Breeding colony](https://www.allaboutbirds.org/guide/Northern_Gannet/photo-gallery/646780637)

Often nests in huge colonies.

[© Justin Flint / Macaulay Library](https://macaulaylibrary.org/video/646780637)Newfoundland and Labrador, June 17, 2022

[![Image 27: Northern Gannet](https://www.allaboutbirds.org/guide/assets/photo/66025341-720px.jpg) ### Immature](https://www.allaboutbirds.org/guide/Northern_Gannet/photo-gallery/66025341)

Immatures have patchy brown and white feathers. They attain adult plumage after 4–5 years. Note long pointed tail and wings.

[© David Disher / Macaulay Library](https://macaulaylibrary.org/photo/43884281)North Carolina, November 01, 2014

[![Image 28: Northern Gannet](https://www.allaboutbirds.org/guide/assets/photo/66025351-720px.jpg) ### Juvenile](https://www.allaboutbirds.org/guide/Northern_Gannet/photo-gallery/66025351)

Note wedge-shaped tail that is often held closed in a point. Juveniles have a dingy belly and a dark tail.

[© Adrien Mauss / Macaulay Library](https://macaulaylibrary.org/photo/64603011)Hauts-de-France, September 07, 2015

[![Image 29: Habitat example of the Northern Gannet](https://www.allaboutbirds.org/guide/assets/photo/66025371-720px.jpg) ### Adult](https://www.allaboutbirds.org/guide/Northern_Gannet/photo-gallery/66025371)

Nests in colonies on cliff ledges and steep slopes.

[© Angus Pritchard / Macaulay Library](https://macaulaylibrary.org/photo/54946321)Scotland, June 26, 2016

[![Image 30: Northern Gannet](https://www.allaboutbirds.org/guide/assets/photo/66025381-720px.jpg) ### Immature and adult](https://www.allaboutbirds.org/guide/Northern_Gannet/photo-gallery/66025381)

Immature birds attain adult plumage after 4–5 years. Note daggerlike bill, narrow black mask, and pale yellow-washed head.

[© Marie O'Neill / Macaulay Library](https://macaulaylibrary.org/photo/60579351)Quebec, June 04, 2017

[![Image 31: Northern Gannet](https://www.allaboutbirds.org/guide/assets/photo/66025361-720px.jpg) ### Habitat](https://www.allaboutbirds.org/guide/Northern_Gannet/photo-gallery/66025361)

Breeds in dense colonies and spends the rest of its time at sea.

[© Lynden Schofield / Macaulay Library](https://macaulaylibrary.org/photo/34041871)Scotland, August 08, 2014

## The Four Keys to ID

*   Size & Shape

A nearly albatross-sized, heavy-bodied seabird, with long, pointed wings, tail, and bill. 

### Relative Size

Larger than a Great Black-backed Gull, smaller than a Brown Pelican.

![Image 40: Relative Size](https://www.allaboutbirds.org/guide/images/size/scale.png)![Image 41: goose or larger](https://www.allaboutbirds.org/guide/images/size/goose-or-larger.png)goose-sized or larger
### Measurements
    *   Male
    *           *   Length: 36.8-43.3 in (93.5-110 cm)
        *   Weight: 87.1-122.4 oz (2470-3470 g)
        *   Wingspan: 70.9-72.4 in (180-184 cm)

    *   Female
    *           *   Length: 36.4-40.9 in (92.5-104 cm)
        *   Weight: 90.7-127.3 oz (2570-3610 g)

![Image 42: Shape of the Northern Gannet](https://www.allaboutbirds.org/guide/assets/photo/66025421-720px.jpg)[© John Reynolds / Macaulay Library](https://macaulaylibrary.org/photo/41713381)

*   Color PatternAdults are snow white with black wingtips and yellow heads; juveniles are uniformly sooty brown; and subadults are intermediate between these plumages, often appearing a patchwork of dark and light feathering. ![Image 43: Color pattern of the Northern Gannet](https://www.allaboutbirds.org/guide/assets/photo/66025391-720px.jpg)[© Dorian Anderson / Macaulay Library](https://macaulaylibrary.org/photo/28586791)  
*   BehaviorNorthern Gannets fly with deep, slow wingbeats as they search for fish, then dive straight down in spectacular plunges, sometimes alone, sometimes in very large flocks. They nest on oceanside cliffs, the only time they set feet on dry land. [Video 1](https://vimeo.com/927297523) [© Timothy Barksdale / Macaulay Library](https://macaulaylibrary.org/video/405110)   
*   HabitatOpen oceans and occasionally in large bays. Nests on cliffs in Atlantic Canada, Iceland, and Europe. ![Image 44: Habitat example of the Northern Gannet](https://www.allaboutbirds.org/guide/assets/photo/66025371-720px.jpg)[© Angus Pritchard / Macaulay Library](https://macaulaylibrary.org/photo/54946321)

[![Image 21: Shape of the Northern Gannet](https://www.allaboutbirds.org/guide/assets/photo/66025421-720px.jpg) ### Adult](https://www.allaboutbirds.org/guide/Northern_Gannet/photo-gallery/66025421)

Large heavy-bodied seabird with a daggerlike bill. Adults are mostly white with a yellowish wash on the head and neck and black flight feathers.

[© John Reynolds / Macaulay Library](https://macaulaylibrary.org/photo/41713381)Occitanie, December 03, 2016

[![Image 22: Northern Gannet](https://www.allaboutbirds.org/guide/assets/photo/66025411-720px.jpg) ### Juvenile](https://www.allaboutbirds.org/guide/Northern_Gannet/photo-gallery/66025411)

Large seabird. Juveniles are brown overall with white spotting.

[© John Reynolds / Macaulay Library](https://macaulaylibrary.org/photo/41713461)Occitanie, December 03, 2016

[![Image 23: Northern Gannet](https://www.allaboutbirds.org/guide/assets/videoThumbs/360242481-720px.jpg) ### Courtship](https://www.allaboutbirds.org/guide/Northern_Gannet/photo-gallery/360242481)

Pairs are monogamous and mate for life. They maintain pair bonds by performing a variety of displays each time they reunite at the nest site.

[© Frédérick Lelièvre / Macaulay Library](https://macaulaylibrary.org/video/360242481)Quebec, July 21, 2021

[![Image 24: Color pattern of the Northern Gannet](https://www.allaboutbirds.org/guide/assets/photo/66025391-720px.jpg) ### Adult](https://www.allaboutbirds.org/guide/Northern_Gannet/photo-gallery/66025391)

Bullet-shaped seabird with long pointed wings and long tail. In flight note white body and black flight feathers.

[© Dorian Anderson / Macaulay Library](https://macaulaylibrary.org/photo/28586791)Newfoundland and Labrador, July 02, 2013

[![Image 25: Northern Gannet](https://www.allaboutbirds.org/guide/assets/photo/66025401-720px.jpg) ### Juvenile](https://www.allaboutbirds.org/guide/Northern_Gannet/photo-gallery/66025401)

Juveniles in flight are brown overall with a white patch on the tail.

[© John Reynolds / Macaulay Library](https://macaulaylibrary.org/photo/41713571)Occitanie, December 03, 2016

[![Image 26: Northern Gannet](https://www.allaboutbirds.org/guide/assets/videoThumbs/646780637-720px.jpg) ### Breeding colony](https://www.allaboutbirds.org/guide/Northern_Gannet/photo-gallery/646780637)

Often nests in huge colonies.

[© Justin Flint / Macaulay Library](https://macaulaylibrary.org/video/646780637)Newfoundland and Labrador, June 17, 2022

[![Image 27: Northern Gannet](https://www.allaboutbirds.org/guide/assets/photo/66025341-720px.jpg) ### Immature](https://www.allaboutbirds.org/guide/Northern_Gannet/photo-gallery/66025341)

Immatures have patchy brown and white feathers. They attain adult plumage after 4–5 years. Note long pointed tail and wings.

[© David Disher / Macaulay Library](https://macaulaylibrary.org/photo/43884281)North Carolina, November 01, 2014

[![Image 28: Northern Gannet](https://www.allaboutbirds.org/guide/assets/photo/66025351-720px.jpg) ### Juvenile](https://www.allaboutbirds.org/guide/Northern_Gannet/photo-gallery/66025351)

Note wedge-shaped tail that is often held closed in a point. Juveniles have a dingy belly and a dark tail.

[© Adrien Mauss / Macaulay Library](https://macaulaylibrary.org/photo/64603011)Hauts-de-France, September 07, 2015

[![Image 29: Habitat example of the Northern Gannet](https://www.allaboutbirds.org/guide/assets/photo/66025371-720px.jpg) ### Adult](https://www.allaboutbirds.org/guide/Northern_Gannet/photo-gallery/66025371)

Nests in colonies on cliff ledges and steep slopes.

[© Angus Pritchard / Macaulay Library](https://macaulaylibrary.org/photo/54946321)Scotland, June 26, 2016

[![Image 30: Northern Gannet](https://www.allaboutbirds.org/guide/assets/photo/66025381-720px.jpg) ### Immature and adult](https://www.allaboutbirds.org/guide/Northern_Gannet/photo-gallery/66025381)

Immature birds attain adult plumage after 4–5 years. Note daggerlike bill, narrow black mask, and pale yellow-washed head.

[© Marie O'Neill / Macaulay Library](https://macaulaylibrary.org/photo/60579351)Quebec, June 04, 2017

[![Image 31: Northern Gannet](https://www.allaboutbirds.org/guide/assets/photo/66025361-720px.jpg) ### Habitat](https://www.allaboutbirds.org/guide/Northern_Gannet/photo-gallery/66025361)

Breeds in dense colonies and spends the rest of its time at sea.

[© Lynden Schofield / Macaulay Library](https://macaulaylibrary.org/photo/34041871)Scotland, August 08, 2014

## The Four Keys to ID

*   Size & Shape

A nearly albatross-sized, heavy-bodied seabird, with long, pointed wings, tail, and bill. 

### Relative Size

Larger than a Great Black-backed Gull, smaller than a Brown Pelican.

![Image 40: Relative Size](https://www.allaboutbirds.org/guide/images/size/scale.png)![Image 41: goose or larger](https://www.allaboutbirds.org/guide/images/size/goose-or-larger.png)goose-sized or larger
### Measurements
    *   Male
    *           *   Length: 36.8-43.3 in (93.5-110 cm)
        *   Weight: 87.1-122.4 oz (2470-3470 g)
        *   Wingspan: 70.9-72.4 in (180-184 cm)

    *   Female
    *           *   Length: 36.4-40.9 in (92.5-104 cm)
        *   Weight: 90.7-127.3 oz (2570-3610 g)

![Image 42: Shape of the Northern Gannet](https://www.allaboutbirds.org/guide/assets/photo/66025421-720px.jpg)[© John Reynolds / Macaulay Library](https://macaulaylibrary.org/photo/41713381)

*   Color PatternAdults are snow white with black wingtips and yellow heads; juveniles are uniformly sooty brown; and subadults are intermediate between these plumages, often appearing a patchwork of dark and light feathering. ![Image 43: Color pattern of the Northern Gannet](https://www.allaboutbirds.org/guide/assets/photo/66025391-720px.jpg)[© Dorian Anderson / Macaulay Library](https://macaulaylibrary.org/photo/28586791)  
*   BehaviorNorthern Gannets fly with deep, slow wingbeats as they search for fish, then dive straight down in spectacular plunges, sometimes alone, sometimes in very large flocks. They nest on oceanside cliffs, the only time they set feet on dry land. [Video 1](https://vimeo.com/927297523) [© Timothy Barksdale / Macaulay Library](https://macaulaylibrary.org/video/405110)   
*   HabitatOpen oceans and occasionally in large bays. Nests on cliffs in Atlantic Canada, Iceland, and Europe. ![Image 44: Habitat example of the Northern Gannet](https://www.allaboutbirds.org/guide/assets/photo/66025371-720px.jpg)[© Angus Pritchard / Macaulay Library](https://macaulaylibrary.org/photo/54946321)
